page: Microsoft Azure E8ps_v5 is a memory-optimized virtual machine built on Microsoft Hyper-V virtualization. The instance features an arm64 architecture powered by Ampere ARMv8 Neoverse-N1 processors running at 3.0 GHz. It allocates 8 dedicated physical cores with 1 thread per core, totaling 8 vCPUs. Cache resources include 64 KB of L1 data cache, 1.0 MB of L2 cache, and 32 MB of shared L3 cache. Memory sizing is configured with 64.0 GB of RAM, yielding a high ratio of 8.0 GB per vCPU. The instance does not include integrated local disk storage or hardware GPU accelerators.

Benchmark performance reveals balanced multi-threaded throughput paired with modest single-thread capacity. In stress-ng testing, the instance achieved 1822.39 on single-core and 14507.4 on multi-core operations, both ranking within the average middle tier. Memory subsystem testing logged 565.27 GB/sec for small-block cached reads, 74.12 GB/sec for large-block uncached reads, and 43.18 GB/sec for uncached writes. Geekbench results include a single-core score of 1056.0 and a multi-core score of 5939.0, reflecting lower execution efficiency in tasks like image and text processing. Compression performance is mixed, with gzip single-threaded rates at 24.06 GB/sec, contrasted with weak bzip3 decompression at 7.32 GB/sec single-threaded and 34.54 GB/sec multi-threaded.

Hardware-level cryptography features standard AES acceleration, delivering 1293.29 on PassMark CPU encryption tests, though it lacks x86-specific vector extensions such as AVX-512 or AMX instructions. Consequently, deep learning workloads exhibit limitations; LLM inference rates register at 242.55 tokens/sec for small model prompt processing and 7.64 tokens/sec for medium model text generation. In network and serving operations, the instance sustains 10.41 GB/sec in static web serving throughput and handles 11.24 million operations/sec in Redis SET operations.

The 8:1 memory-to-vCPU ratio and dedicated core model provide solid cost efficiency for memory-heavy services that do not require intensive compute bursts. It is well-matched for in-memory caching solutions like Redis, relational database hosting, static web traffic handling, and general-purpose ARM-native software compilation pipelines.
